reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / GOLD & ATS guidelines
clinicalPearls: Characterised by repetitive collapse of the upper airway during sleep, producing apnoeas and hypopnoeas with recurrent oxygen desaturations and arousals
Typical features include loud habitual snoring, witnessed breathing pauses, choking or gasping at night, and unrefreshing sleep
Excessive daytime sleepiness, morning headache, poor concentration, and mood disturbance are common daytime consequences
Obesity, increased neck circumference, male sex, retrognathia, and enlarged tonsils are important predisposing factors
Polysomnography is the diagnostic standard, with severity graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index; home sleep testing can be used in selected patients
Continuous positive airway pressure is the mainstay of therapy for moderate-to-severe disease, splinting the airway open during sleep
Weight reduction, avoidance of alcohol and sedatives, positional therapy, and treatment of nasal obstruction are useful adjuncts
Untreated OSA is linked to hypertension, arrhythmias, ischaemic heart disease, stroke, insulin resistance, and increased motor-vehicle accident risk
reference.pathophysiology: During sleep, reduced tone of the pharyngeal dilator muscles allows the anatomically narrowed or collapsible upper airway to close, producing partial (hypopnoea) or complete (apnoea) obstruction despite continued respiratory effort. The resulting hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, and rising respiratory effort trigger brief cortical arousals that restore airway patency but fragment sleep. Recurrent cycles of desaturation-reoxygenation and arousal drive sympathetic activation, surges in blood pressure, oxidative stress, and systemic inflammation, which over time contribute to cardiovascular and metabolic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Insufficient sleep or poor sleep hygiene
additionalInvestigations: In-laboratory polysomnography to confirm diagnosis and grade severity
Home sleep apnoea testing in appropriately selected patients without significant comorbidity
Overnight or nocturnal oximetry as a screening adjunct
Validated questionnaires and sleepiness scales to assess pretest probability and symptom burden
Assessment for associated conditions including hypertension, thyroid dysfunction, and metabolic disease
redFlags: Severe daytime sleepiness in occupational drivers or machine operators posing safety risk
Signs of daytime hypoventilation or right heart failure suggesting overlap with hypoventilation syndromes
Rapidly progressive symptoms or marked nocturnal desaturation
reference.prognosis: With consistent adherence to positive airway pressure and weight management, symptoms and quality of life usually improve markedly and cardiovascular risk is reduced; poorly controlled or untreated disease carries substantial long-term cardiovascular, metabolic, and accident-related morbidity.
pitfalls: Attributing daytime sleepiness solely to lifestyle and missing significant OSA
Overlooking OSA as a driver of resistant hypertension or atrial fibrillation
Assuming all patients are obese; OSA can occur with normal body habitus due to craniofacial anatomy
Failing to address poor CPAP adherence, which undermines treatment benefit
management: Continuous positive airway pressure as the mainstay for moderate-to-severe disease, splinting the upper airway open during sleep
Weight reduction and lifestyle measures, including avoidance of alcohol and sedatives before sleep
Mandibular advancement devices for mild-to-moderate disease or CPAP intolerance
Positional therapy and treatment of nasal obstruction as adjuncts
Upper airway or bariatric surgery in selected patients, including adenotonsillectomy where enlarged tonsils are causative
Management of associated conditions such as hypertension, metabolic disease and thyroid dysfunction
Advice on driving safety, with monitoring of therapy adherence and residual daytime symptoms

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of Obstructive sleep apnoea

nodes.text: Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness
Red flag present (dangerous sleepiness, hypoventilation, right heart failure)?
Advise against driving while dangerously sleepy; urgent review if heart failure
Polysomnography or home testing, gas exchange, cardiac review if severe
Repetitive upper airway collapse with desaturations on polysomnography?
Consider central apnoea or narcolepsy; refer for sleep medicine
CPAP as the mainstay for moderate-to-severe disease
Weight reduction to improve the airway
Safety advice about sleepiness and driving
With CPAP adherence and weight control, symptoms and quality of life improve markedly
